newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Rifle grenedes fired in Bosnian town, IPTF says.
newsitem.headline: Rifle grenedes fired in Bosnian town, IPTF says.

text.p: International police monitors expressed alarm on Friday over rising tension in the divided Bosnian town of Mostar a day after seven explosions rocked the town centre.

Two rifle grenades were fired at an apartment building in the Croat-held western part of Mostar on Thursday evening, Frank Sarver, a spokesman for the International Police Task Force (IPTF), said by telephone.
"One hit the side of the building on about the seventh floor and put a hole in it. The second one fell short in front of the building," Sarver told Reuters.
U.N. police monitors also reported five explosions along the former front line in Mostar, but the source of the explosions remained unclear, Sarver said.
IPTF was concerned over the incidents and planned to step up patrols to try discourage further violence, Sarver said.
A spokesman for the NATO-led Stabilisation Force (SFOR), which polices the peace agreement in Bosnia, called the explosions "alarming".
But Major Tony White said SFOR had no plans to increase patrols or change its approach to peacekeeping in the area.
Croats and Moslems, who began the Bosnian conflict as allies against Serb forces, waged a vicious 10-month war that ended in February 1994.
The Moslem-Croat fighting devastated Mostar and the ancient Ottoman town remains strictly divided between Moslem and Croat sectors.
Croat media, controlled by local Croat authorities, quickly blamed Moslems in eastern Mostar for the explosions.
This week's violence -- the worst in several months -- coincided with fierce political disputes between rival Croat and Moslem leaders in Mostar and elsewhere.

The office of the international High Repesentative to Bosnia said hardline elements opposed to reunifying Mostar have been trying for some time to disrupt reconciliation and promote hostility between rival Moslem and Croat communities.
"When we have (political) tensions you have people who want to add fuel to the fire," said Dragan Gasic, spokesman for the Mostar office of the High Representative.
The newly-elected municipal government charged with reunifying Mostar has no offices because Croat nationalists have occupied the building which was supposed to house the new administration.
A meeting of the cantonal government for the Mostar region ended in bitter disagreement on Thursday, with Moslem and Croat representatives unable to agree on a budget.
In Sarajevo, Croat deputies walked out of a session of the Moslem-Croat federation government on Thursday to protest against proposals for power-sharing inside the federation.
